intro: A German adjective can stand after a verb or directly before a noun. Its form depends on where it appears.

lessons.title: After sein, werden, or bleiben
lessons.label: No adjective ending
lessons.note: When the adjective describes the subject after these verbs, it stays in its basic form.

lessons.title: Before a noun
lessons.label: Add an ending
lessons.note: The ending changes with the article, gender, number, and case. Start with these nominative examples; use the Cases Master for the full charts.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.label: Comparative and superlative

examples.german: Heute ist der Bus schneller als der Zug.
examples.english: Today the bus is faster than the train.

examples.german: Der Zug ist so schnell wie der Bus.
examples.english: The train is as fast as the bus.

lessons.note: Many adjectives add -er and -sten. Some add an umlaut, and some forms are irregular.

lessons.title: Learn the common irregular forms
lessons.label: Worth memorizing
lessons.note: Do not add the regular endings to these forms.

lessons.title: Describe a thing or a person
lessons.label: Mind the meaning

examples.german: Ich bin an dem Film interessiert.
examples.english: I am interested in the film.

lessons.note: Interessant describes what causes interest; interessiert describes the person who feels it.

caution: The list pairs each adjective with a useful contrast or partner. Not every word has a perfect one-word opposite, and colours are grouped by contrast for easier recall.
